# Kuddālajātaka (Ja 70)

**ID:** Ja 70
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kuddālajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Spade Sage
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja70
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kuddālajātaka* (Ja 70) is the tenth and concluding story of the seventh chapter (*Itthivagga*) in the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877]. Its opening frame (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana and concerns the monk Cittahattha-Sāriputta, who left the monastic order six times before finally mastering the seven books of the Abhidhamma, winning discernment, and attaining arahantship upon his seventh entry [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. 

To explain that a future awakened being could also struggle with worldly attachments, the Buddha relates the story of his past life as Kuddālapaṇḍita [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877]. In this past birth, the Bodhisatta was repeatedly drawn away from the ascetic life back to household existence on six occasions because of an attachment to a single blunt spade he used for tilling the soil [Burlingame 1921]. Determined to abandon this temptation once and for all, he threw the spade with closed eyes into the Ganges and shouted, "I have conquered!" [Burlingame 1921]. The King of Benares, returning victorious from a military campaign, heard the exclamation; Kuddālapaṇḍita explained that political and military conquests must be fought repeatedly, whereas conquering the internal enemy of desire is final and supreme [Burlingame 1921; Lang 2003]. Moved by this teaching, the king and his retinue abandoned their possessions to take up the ascetic life in the Himavanta, where Sakka had the architect Vissakamma construct a hermitage [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877]. The narrative concludes with the identification of the king as Ānanda and Kuddāla as the Buddha [Fausböll 1877]. Modern scholarship notes how the tale highlights themes of possessionlessness, using the Bodhisatta's attachment to an item of negligible value to critique the structural values of property, status, and sensual pursuit [Fenn 1994].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external parallels or automated text-reuse matches for this jātaka in other Buddhist corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The narrative also appears in synoptic form in the Dhammapada commentary [Burlingame 1921].

- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1 (1921) — Provided the narrative synopsis of Kuddāla and his blunt spade as preserved in the Dhammapada commentary.
